name: Eye area ratio

lead: Eye area ratio refers to the proportions people measure around the eyes: the angle of the eye corners (canthal tilt), the distance between the eyes relative to eye width, the shape and height of the eye opening (palpebral fissure), and the gap between brow and lid. Looksmaxxing forums use these numbers to describe what makes an eye area look the way it does.

The payoff is diagnostic: once someone can name the feature they want to change, they can choose between options such as brow grooming, eyeliner or lash styling, eyelid or canthus procedures, or simply photo angles. Published anatomy and aesthetics literature describes eye landmarks and facial symmetry, but community targets are mostly informal.

paras: People photograph the face straight-on in even light, mark landmarks such as the inner and outer corners of the eye, pupils and brow, and compare the measurements with the ranges they consider ideal. Forum members post photos and ask what to fix, then discuss options ranging from grooming and makeup to surgical canthoplasty.

The main risk is acting on measurements that are sensitive to camera angle, lens distortion and expression, which can lead to choices based on inaccurate readings. Any surgical option around the eyes carries the usual operative risks and should be discussed with a qualified surgeon.

angle.text: The ratios themselves change nothing; they are a measuring system that lets people pick a targeted change for the eye region. Users compare their numbers with community ranges and then decide whether brows, makeup, lashes or a procedure fits.

lead: Eye area ratios are the measurements and proportions of the periorbital region that looksmaxxers use to describe and compare eyes. Typical items include canthal tilt (the angle of the line from the inner to the outer corner of the eye), the width of the eye relative to the distance between the eyes, the height of the eye opening, and the distance from brow to lid [1].

The point of tracking them is to turn a general impression of the eyes into specific, changeable features. Someone who sees a negative canthal tilt or a large brow-to-lid gap in photographs can then look at options aimed at that feature, from makeup and brow shaping to canthoplasty. In forum threads, members post front-facing photos and ask what to correct about their eye area and ratios [1].

Anatomically, the inner and outer canthi are the ends of the palpebral fissure, and cephalometric analysis uses the endocanthion and exocanthion landmarks to represent them [2]. Research on facial attractiveness has focused on symmetry, averageness and youthfulness, which are discussed in the wider literature [3].

paras: Canthal tilt describes whether the outer corner of the eye sits higher than the inner corner (positive tilt), level, or lower (negative tilt). Interocular or eye-spacing ratios compare the gap between the eyes with the width of one eye. Fissure measurements describe the height and length of the eye opening, and brow measurements describe the gap between brow and upper lid.

The canthi are the corners where the eyelids meet, and the bicanthal plane links them. East Asian eyes often have the inner canthus partly covered by an epicanthal fold, which is one reason eye proportions differ between populations [2].

On looksmax.org, users post threads asking how to fix their eye area and ratios, citing features such as a negative canthal tilt, and receive suggestions from other members that range from surgery to cosmetic changes [1]. The vocabulary is part of broader facial-analysis discussion, which also covers symmetry and proportion [3].

Studies of facial attractiveness report that symmetry, averageness and youthfulness influence ratings, though researchers caution that some symmetry experiments create artificial features by mirroring faces [3]. The specific ratios and ideal ranges used in forums are not drawn from a single standardised published system.
No studies found. Related literature exists on lateral canthoplasty and epicanthus surgery, but no clinical study evaluates the community's eye-area ratio framework itself.

claims.claim: Eye ratios such as canthal tilt largely determine how attractive the eye area looks
